EntertainmentTab.title: The 50 best TV shows to watch this autumn
EntertainmentTab.text:
Wayward and chaotic, in the grand tradition of The Word and TFI Friday, Late Night Lycett proved that Joe Lycett had fully inherited Friday nights on Channel 4. Its follow-up sounds even more TFI-esque. The Lycett Arms is a real east London pub, open for just one hour a week, which required Lycett to train to be accredited with a level 2 award for personal licence holders. The show promises “top-drawer comedy entertainment from Joe and a pub full of celebrity guests”. What could possibly go wrong?

Channel 4, 4 September

Colin from Accounts’ Patrick Brammall is totally changing tack with this intense drama about a one-time cop whose three-year-old daughter Mags disappeared more than a decade ago. When the remains of a young girl are found nearby, Ian Ridley (Brammall) is first on the scene – and his former colleagues in the police force know there’s nothing they can do to stop him from doing some digging. But the truth about the victim is far murkier. A twisty six-parter that will keep you guessing.

Apple TV, 9 September

Jackson’s Joes are being picked off one by one – and everyone who has ever worked at Slough House has been wiped from the system at MI5 HQ the Park, so no one will even know they’re goners. The sixth season of the smash-hit drama about supposedly second-rate spies kicks off with a horrifying fire in a shipping container and a very violent funeral, and only ramps up from there. The usual suspects, from Gary Oldman and Kristin Scott Thomas to Jack Lowden, are still at it. Plus, the brilliant Lenny Rush joins the cast – and turns out to be a dab hand at spycraft.

Apple TV, 16 September

“Has any man ever said: ‘Have you met my girlfriend? She’s sexy, she’s fun, she’s 60.’ I need to meet someone now. I think I’ve got 10 years left as a sexual person, tops.” Sharon Horgan’s new comedy is as scabrous and hilarious as always. Things aren’t going great for Alex (played by Horgan herself): her body is failing her, her son Ruari is veering off the rails (mooning at his school graduation) and her ex is moving abroad, leaving her even more of a single parent. Let’s hope she’s able to spice things up with some “new dick energy”.

HBO Max, 20 September

First Woody Harrelson and Matthew McConaughey starred in True Detective. Then McConaughey revealed that he recently discovered he might have the same father as Harrelson. And now, bizarrely, they are basically Curb Your Enthusiasming this new dynamic. In Brothers, the pair play fictionalised versions of themselves who learn that … well, you can see where this is going. You have to applaud the effort, since making an entire television series about some family gossip seems like so much more hard work than simply getting a DNA test.

Apple TV, 23 September

Strictly Come Dancing

All eyes on the Elstree and Borehamwood ballroom for the first series of the sparkly dance staple without Claudia Winkleman and Tess Daly. How on earth will the trio of new hosts – former pro dancer and all-round icon Johannes Radebe, Emma “safe pair of hands” Willis and comedian and former penguin suit-wearing Christmas contestant Josh Widdicombe – fare? And will any other scandals befall the show as it attempts this reset? The contestants include Shaun Wright-Phillips, Jaime Winstone, Dani Dyer, Delta Goodrem and, er, celebrity hair stylist Chris Appleton.

BBC One, September

The Great British Bake Off

Stale no more! Bake Off has been in serious need of a revamp for a while now – and who better to zhuzh it up than the queen of sass herself, Nigella Lawson. The grande dame of spoon-licking cookery TV, and all-time winner of best pronunciation of the word microwavay, joins as the new judge. Expect to be whisked away by her charm, withering putdowns and (fingers crossed) fantastic repartee with Paul Hollywood.

Channel 4, September

Well, this one looks bonkers. Catherine Zeta-Jones plays a former international cocaine dealer who has spent 20 years hiding in plain sight as an ostentatiously wealthy art dealer. But her cover is blown when she discovers that a group of elite assassins called the Seven Demons has been hired to kill her. Needless to say, she tries to kill them first. Co-starring Daniel Ings, Julian Barratt and Julian Rhind-Tutt, this has the potential to be the most entertaining thing in forever.

Prime Video, 2 October

It’s juicy, it’s bitchy and it’s very starry indeed: George Kay’s tentpole divorce drama looks at the bitter end of a relationship from both sides, meeting the lawyers making cases for all parties. Here, the movie star and tech billionaire going through proceedings are played by Sienna Miller and Dominic West. The cast is absolutely stacked, from reunited Celebrity Traitors mates Nick Mohammed and Celia Imrie (who could forget when he dug up her grave?) to Aran Murphy (son of Cillian – and set to be everywhere on our screens) as the feuding couple’s son.

Sky/Now, 2 October

Last One Laughing Halloween special

Last One Laughing is such an ingenious money-maker – a whole series spun out from putting some comedians in a room for less than a day! – that we were always going to get more of it. While we await the third series (which stars Harry Hill!) this Halloween special features Jack Dee, Phil Wang, Reece Shearsmith, Harriet Dyer and Tom Allen, alongside the returning Lou Sanders and Daisy May Cooper, and there’s an intriguing new rule: competitors will be punished not just for laughing, but also for screaming.

Prime Video, 23 October

Rowan Joffé has long been a writer worth paying attention to, most recently for Edward Berger’s film Ballad of a Small Player. Nocturne sounds like it might cement his reputation once and for all. A drama about a homicide cop who relocates to Pennsylvania and finds himself having to deal with a serial killer, it stars Liev Schreiber and Zazie Beetz. Best of all, Stephen Graham plays the serial killer. Entertaining grisliness should ensue.

Apple TV, 30 October

Television loves to adapt real-life things that have only just happened, and that’s the case with The Altruists, which deals with the rise (and subsequent implosion) of cryptocurrency exchange FTX. This is the one where Sam Bankman-Fried came out of nowhere to become the 41st richest man in the US, only to get sentenced to 25 years in jail for fraud, conspiracy and money laundering. When this genre gets it right, it makes for gripping TV. When it gets it wrong, it leaves you wondering why you didn’t just read the Wikipedia page. Fingers crossed for the former.

Netflix, 19 November

After two dazzling big-screen outings (neither of which were commercially successful at the time) comes the inevitable TV adaptation. Set 80 years after the original, and 50 since the sequel, Blade Runner 2099 revolves round the aftermath of a Replicant uprising. Michelle Yeoh plays a dying Replicant Blade Runner. Hunter Schafer plays a human pretending to be a replicant. The amount of money thrown at this thing must be staggering, not least because the production design looks absolutely gorgeous. A must-see.

Prime Video, 25 November

Where can TV’s most rollicking bonkfest possibly go after part one of this second series ended harrowingly in the 1987 hurricane – and denied us the queer epiphany we’d all been waiting for? As we return to Rutshire, will Lizzie actually leave her abominable husband? Will Declan find out his wife Maud slept with his sworn enemy? Will Taggie ever move on from Rupert Campbell-Black? Expect sex, more sex, some gleefully evil regional TV wars and at least one funeral.

Both anticipation and trepidation are high for the small-screen version of JK Rowling’s wizarding classic. Security has had to be ramped up on set because of intense heat on stars such as Paapa Essiedu (who plays Severus Snape) and John Lithgow (Albus Dumbledore), and there have been calls for actors to quit the project. But the first teaser looks truly epic – and child actors have upped their game since the movies.

HBO Max, Christmas Day

A Bitter Pill: The Sodium Valproate Scandal

Sodium valproate is an effective epilepsy treatment. However, if it is taken during pregnancy, one in nine babies will have a physical birth defect. It is estimated that 20,000 children in the UK were affected. A Bitter Pill (made by the co-producers of Mr Bates vs the Post Office) follows the story of two mothers – Janet Williams and Emma Murphy – who spent decades battling doctors and drug companies to first find answers and then compensation. It is an incredible story of bloody-minded tenacity, and hopefully this documentary will help it reach a wider audience.

A reality show/social experiment in which 16 participants/foolish guinea pigs are dropped in an actual ghost town in the US to see if they could survive the end of days. There will be no electricity or water or any mod cons, and they will be stuck there for a month. Think The Road for the influencer age. Sure to be utterly bananas.

Jen Beagin’s 2023 novel has all the hallmarks of a television adaptation – it’s full of rich people with good taste, almost all of whom have endured some form of terrible trauma – and so it has come to pass. Jodie Comer will star as Flavia, a woman in a sexually unfulfilling marriage who embarks on an affair with a woman she meets at the dog park. However (possible spoiler, although probably not), the woman is secretly employed as her sex therapist’s transcriber. It is a dynamic that cannot possibly hold.

The Ben Whishaw-Keira Knightley spy epic returns for more killer espionage fun with incredible new cast members Ambika Mod, Sam Riley and the Scream queen herself, Neve Campbell. Better still: Sarah Lancashire will have a far more prominent role in season two! Always a reason to celebrate.

The Bafta-winning show about the “peelers” of Blackthorn police station in Belfast always sets out its stall with a stunning set piece in the opener. Season four is no exception, as police are called to a gathering at a migrant centre where multiple far-right groups are converging and ready to attack. Somehow it gets even more gripping and politically on point every time.

It was announced on David Attenborough’s 100th birthday that he would be back to narrate the final part of this world-changing trilogy – and we got a sneak peek of him in his home studio intoning about the mating rituals of a whale. Given that this follows his spectacular feature-length film on the urgency of protecting our oceans to ensure human survival, and that it might well be the last time we hear his honeyed tones adorn something new, this will be totally unmissable. What a way to cap off his centenary year.

The Boys from Brazil

Ira Levin’s bracing Nazi thriller has already been adapted into one masterpiece – the 1978 film starring Gregory Peck and Laurence Olivier – and now it is heading for the small screen. Peter Morgan has adapted the story into a five-part limited series starring Jeremy Strong, Gillian Anderson, Daniel Brühl and Lizzy Caplan. A film about a resurgence of nazism feels painfully relevant, although it remains to be seen how straight the show will play some of the story’s battier sci-fi elements.

Many of us may have experienced the peculiar anguish of being trapped in a tenancy agreement with someone you’ve just broken up with, and this premise forms the spine of the new Channel 4 comedy Break Clause. Lara Ricote and Samuel Bottomley play the couple, working from a script by Jess Bray from the brilliant We Might Regret This. The series originated as a 16-minute Comedy Blap that you can – and should – watch on Channel 4. If the series maintains the charm of the original, this should be something very special.

Mike Flanagan is very much The Stephen King Guy at this stage, having written and directed the 2017 adaptation of Gerald’s Game, the 2019 adaptation of Doctor Sleep and 2024’s The Life of Chuck. And now (while he apparently readies adaptations of The Dark Tower and The Mist) he has adapted Carrie for television. You know the story already – a telekinetic teen with a horrible mother has to navigate school bullies – but this will apparently be an update, complete with modern technology and a sorority of telekinetic girls.

The Celebrity Traitors

We didn’t think it was possible to trump the first lineup of celebrities entering the castle with Claudia – but this year’s casting may just have done it. With superstar luvvies such as Jerry Hall, Richard E Grant and Michael Sheen, double act Rob and Romesh pitted against each other and some tantalising curveballs – what will Ross Kemp, Myha’la and Bella Ramsey possibly chat about? – it’s sure to be another winner. This can’t come soon enough.

Colin from Accounts

What a beautiful thing Colin from Accounts is. A relationship dramedy written by its stars, the husband and wife team of Patrick Brammall and Harriet Dyer, it is a funny and tender exploration of romantic compatibility in the modern age. In season one, Ashley and Gordon met and fell in love. In season two they tried to work out if they should stay together. In its third and final season, we learn that they didn’t. But might they again?

Damilola Taylor: The Last 24 Hours

The murder of 10-year-old Damilola Taylor in a Peckham stairwell 26 years ago has lost none of its horrors with age. One of the last people to see Taylor alive was actor John Boyega, then eight, who was friends with the family. In this documentary, Boyega explores Taylor’s final day, along with other close friends and family members, discussing both the events that led to his death and the impact his murder had on their lives.

Between Baby Reindeer, Somewhere Boy and Misfits, Clerkenwell Films has developed an incredible pedigree when it comes to television. Deadpoint looks primed to continue this. A five-part action thriller set in Wales, it is the story of a man forced back to Snowdonia after the disappearance of his sister, only to discover that a far-right faction is planning to carry out a violent attack there. So it’s a survival thriller, a missing persons mystery and a domestic terrorism drama all in one. What could be better?

You don’t adapt Steinbeck unless you’re willing to go all in on it, and happily this seems to be the case with Netflix’s new show. This epic tale of family, inheritance and jealousy spans decades, and judging by the trailer its writer, Zoe Kazan, has committed entirely. Florence Pugh plays Cathy Ames, the beautiful monster at the story’s heart, with Christopher Abbott, Tracy Letts and Martha Plimpton rounding out the cast. This looks as sumptuous and panoramic as television will allow. On first impressions, it could be an award winner.

Dominic Savage’s semi-improvised I Am … series has drawn some of the best female performers to its flame since it began, including Vicky McClure, Samantha Morton, Lesley Manville and Kate Winslet. Now it is the turn of Nicola Coughlan who (in a break from tradition) is starring in a two-part story. I Am Helen will explore themes of control and toxic masculinity in the setting of a modern relationship. Early reports suggest that it will deal heavily in the manosphere. If it manages to broach this as well as Adolescence did, it might be essential viewing.

A fresh comedy from Leo Reich, whose debut Edinburgh fringe show Literally Who Cares?! was such a barnstorming success that it immediately got picked up by HBO Max. It Gets Worse is a look at three young mates in London who are on the verge of getting evicted. But what’s really staggering here is the sheer number of A-listers who have signed on – from Andrew “hot priest” Scott to Lena Dunham. This should be special.

If you can see a theme emerging in this list, it might be the Big Legacy Television Adaptation. Not being ones to miss out, the BBC has adapted this series from John le Carré’s The Spy Who Came in from the Cold, also drawing on material from his 2017 novel A Legacy of Spies. If nothing else, it has been exquisitely cast, with Matthew Macfadyen playing George Smiley, Charlie Hunnam as Alec Leamas, Hugh Laurie as Control and supporting roles played by Daniel Brühl, Joe Alwyn and Agnes O’Casey.

Daisy Haggard’s writing is always dark and very funny, and her new witness protection thriller Maya is no exception. Anna (Haggard) and her daughter Maya (Bella Ramsey, as wonderful and unrestrained as ever) are forced to leave their home with no notice and move to the back of beyond in Scotland to escape her abusive ex (played by a chilling Tobias Menzies). It’s a moving look at survival and hope, with cliffhangers galore and gags about Frazzles crisps. What’s not to love?

Steven Moffat’s ludicrously anticipated comedy-drama is finally almost here. A workplace show set in Downing Street – starring Rafe Spall as the prime minister, with Jenna Coleman as his deputy chief of staff – it could well be the British West Wing. And given Moffat’s flair for witty dialogue (and his form writing Press Gang), this has the potential to be one of the year’s best. But let’s hope it doesn’t run and run, because at this stage a British prime minister lasting more than a couple of years is nothing short of fantasy.

Finally, David Harewood gets the starring vehicle he deserves. In Pierre, he plays a London duty solicitor described as “charming and funny, a glamorous character in an unglamorous profession”. However, he is forced to step up when he realises that the death of one of his clients might have been the result of a vast institutional cover-up. Pierre sounds like old-school television at its best; a show with something to say, and the smarts to wrap it in an irresistible character.

Pride and Prejudice

“Miss Elizabeth Bennet? I’m all astonishment!”​ There’s long-awaited, and then there’s Dolly Alderton’s update of Pride and Prejudice, which comes with sky-high expectations. Thankfully, Olivia Colman is downright hilarious as ​the busybody Mrs Bennet, determined to marry off ​o​ne of her five daughters to the swanky neighbour who just moved in next door. Emma Corrin stars as Elizabeth and Jack Lowden is heralding himself as the first “ginger” Mr Darcy. We’re promised even more ​s​park than the Colin Firth ​classic from the 90s – though there will be no lake scene.

The Rachel Incident

Based on Caroline O’Donoghue’s 2023 novel, beloved of countless millennial women, this is a new Channel 4 show about a young student’s attempt to seduce her married professor. The cast, including Máiréad Tyers, Ellis Howard, Daniel Ings and Ardal O’Hanlon, is worth getting excited about. But the real draw is the fact that O’Donoghue collaborated on the script with Jen Statsky, fresh from conquering the world with Hacks. If she can bring even a hint of the same sparkle to this, we will be in for a treat.

The Reluctant Vampire

“You don’t pick up being a vampire … it’s not conversational French!” Valentine hates drinking blood, ​has no truck with violence and –​ horror of horrors –​ he has a reflection. But his vampire family still don’t know he’s actually a human and they want him to pass his initiation ceremony in front of the whole community of Katchem-By-the-Throat. This BBC comedy from the Gibbons brothers (renowned for keeping Alan Partridge alive), based on a book by Eric Morecambe, has an incredibly high gag rate and a cracking cast​. It ​includes​ Lenny Rush as the titular non-vamp, ​Sian Clifford and Tom Davis as his parents, Asim Chaudhry as Igon the family assistant and Bill Bailey and Ross ​Noble as ​a hilarious pair of gargoyles​.

Well this one sounds like fun. Written by Anya Reiss and starring Naomie Harris and Christina Hendricks, Reputation is a glossy drama about a celebrity lawsuit that spirals out of control. A pop star writes a song accusing her husband of infidelity. He fires accusations back. Social media goes wild, and a phalanx of dirty PR tricks comes into play. The enjoyment won’t just come from seeing the inner workings of the lawsuits we only hear about in the news, but presumably also trying to guess which precise celebrity lawsuits the show is based on.

The Secret Diary of Adrian Mole Aged 13¾

There aren’t many characters in literature more beloved than Sue Townsend’s self-importantly earnest adolescent, whose diaries enthralled a nation across four decades and eight books. After 1985’s classic ITV adaptation, David Nicholls has come on board to bring him back to life as a period piece. Writers for this new version include Caitlin and Caroline Moran, Dillon Mapletoft, Oliver Taylor and Jack Rooke, while Oliver Savell from Changing Ends will play the lead. Can lightning strike twice?

One of the most seminal documentaries ever made finally concludes. Since 1964, the Up series has followed the lives of several perfectly normal people across the social spectrum at increments of seven years. Through the decades, the participants have fallen in love and endured hardships, and now they are almost at the end of the road. The final chapter – directed by the Oscar-winning Asif Kapadia after the death of Michael Apted – is bound to be poignant, but the series as a whole will remain an important document about life in Britain in the 20th and 21st centuries for ever.

Fresh from his job consulting on SNL UK, of all things, James Graham gets back to his masterwork. In its two series so far, Sherwood has been an almost unbearably dark investigation of a community left to hold itself together with threads. Six months have passed since the climax of season two, in which evil matriarch Ann Branson drowned, yet more human remains have been found. Who in the town has a dark secret this time?

The Slightest Touch

A documentary in which Colin Farrell meets up with his friend and discusses running a marathon. The catch is that his friend is Emma Fogarty, a survivor of epidermolysis bullosa, a rare and painful genetic condition that renders the skin fragile enough to blister and tear at the slightest touch. Fogarty has already confounded medical science once before – she was never expected to reach the age of 40 – so why not go the whole hog and run the Dublin marathon? Powerfully emotional and uplifting in equal measure.

Over its three series (and Christmas special), Abi Morgan’s divorce drama The Split became one of the highlights of the annual schedule. Rather than ending, it has now morphed into The Split Up. This is a new, Manchester-set series about a powerful family struggling to decide who should inherit its prestigious divorce firm. Morgan is just executive producing this one, handing the reins to Ursula Rani Sarma. Ritu Arya, Sanjeev Bhaskar, Aysha Kala and Arian Nik star.

The first season of this swaggering Liverpool gangland thriller didn’t quite get the dues it deserved (that rooftop scene in the finale was gasp-inducing), but it did establish James Nelson-Joyce – who got his big break after chatting to his idol Stephen Graham at Nando’s – as a swiftly rising star. He returns for more explosive drama, as well as Endeavour star Shaun Evans, who joins the cast.

Jimmy McGovern’s prison anthology has so far been absolutely gripping. And now, following runs led by Sean Bean and Jodie Whittaker, David Tennant gets a turn at the wheel. This story is set at a young offenders institution, and Tennant plays a custodial manager concealing knowledge about a serious incident. As connective tissue, Siobhan Finneran returns as prison chaplain Marie-Louise O’Dell, now undergoing a crisis of faith, who clashes with Tennant over it.

The Unlikely Cook With Awkwafina

Once a mainstay of the television schedules, the food show has lost no end of ground to YouTube in recent years. Perhaps this series is the thing to regain it. In The Unlikely Cook With Awkwafina, the titular star will travel across the US exploring modern Asian-American cuisine. Why is Awkwafina an unlikely cook? Because she is apparently extremely unskilled in the kitchen and will have to rely on a host of people more talented (but less famous) than she is to show her the way.

Picture this: Michael Gove is the prime minister. Nicola Sturgeon is his deputy. His cabinet comprises Penny Mordaunt, Baroness Harman, Baroness Warsi and Kim Darroch, while Anthony Scaramucci plays the US secretary of state. If that doesn’t sound awful enough, Russia has just invaded the UK. Welcome to The Wargame, a series where these figures enter a Cobra-style briefing room and attempt to deal with the minute-by-minute developments of such a crisis. This could be gripping or it could be the television equivalent of banging yourself on the head with a tin tray. Either way, it will probably be worth watching.

Few things have been as flat-out terrifying as Danny Robbins’s podcast The Witch Farm, about the supposedly true haunting of an isolated Welsh farmhouse 30 years ago. Now the podcast has been made into a TV show. If it can cram as many unsettling incidents as the podcast – think apparitions, dead animals and unusually high utility bills – while maintaining its tone of sceptical unease, this will hands down be the scariest thing on television in several years.

AKA what Heated Rivalry’s Hudson Williams did next. He stars alongside Carrie-Anne Moss and Noah Reid in a raunchy and ritualistic take on the terrifying folklore tale of Baba Yaga. It should fall somewhere between Jodie Foster’s True Detective: Night Country and a wildly freewheeling fairytale.

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘I’m an ever-changing vessel’: Erykah Badu on defying definition, life as a birth and death doula and her first album in 11 years
EntertainmentTab.text:
Erykah Badu needs the lights down low. The singer, producer, actor and registered doula shuffles into a private room at London’s Soho hotel and quietly asks for some changes to the atmosphere: lights dimmed, soft seat. A green juice would be great.

As it turns out, Badu was out last night with Dave Chappelle, sitting with the comedian at a grand piano and playing songs into the wee hours. She looks mischievous when she thinks about the impromptu party, but declines to go into detail about what, exactly, went on. Instead, the 55-year-old smiles at me, eyes wide, her gold teeth glinting in the low light: “Oh yes,” she says slowly and quietly, like some kind of mysterious warlock. “It was a late one …”

Meeting Badu, in other words, is everything you want it to be and more. She and I are here to talk about Before the World Blows: The Abi and Alan Experiment, a collaborative record with famed underground producer the Alchemist. It’s Badu’s first full-length project since the release of 2015’s But You Caint Use My Phone mixtape, and its dense, layered sound feels like an internet-fried take on her era-defining New Amerykah albums, from 2008 and 2010.

It’s surprising, I suggest, that she has taken so long between records, given how much she analyses the world around her. She says that’s the point. “Procrastinating and living, learning and stuff – that gives you stuff to write about,” she says. “It’s important to gather the data, upload as much as I can. I don’t have a choice. But when the thing gets kind of full, I download it through writing music.”

Badu has been a star since 1997, when the release of her debut album, Baduizm, announced her as one of the leading lights of what music industry executive Kedar Massenburg called “neo soul”, a new wave of alternative soul and R&B. In the years since, a handful of wild, boundary-pushing records have made Badu one of the most revered artists in the world. The Alchemist – LA producer Alan Maman – was one of those early fans. In 1997, he was a roadie for Cypress Hill, who were co-headlining the Smokin’ Grooves tour alongside Badu. “I was such a fan – I used to go out in the crowd and watch her show every night,” he says on the phone later. “I never would have thought in a million years that one day I would be making music with her.”

Since then, Maman has produced a number of hits, including Mobb Deep’s 1999 track The Realest, and enjoyed a recent career renaissance in collaborations with underground rappers such as the duos Armand Hammer and Mike & Wiki. A few years ago, while DJing a party, he ran into an old friend named Cold Cris who happened to work for Badu, and told him that working with her was on his bucket list. Two years after that, he got the call that Badu was interested in playing around with his beats. She came to his studio in LA, and the pair, he says, “instantly became friends, and realised how much shit we had in common, in the way we create, the way we think”.

“His compositions are like classical music to me – how he layers chimes and voices and strings and horns,” says Badu. “Our process is the same. The way we build is the same. I don’t know what it is exactly, but it’s a burning, beautiful fire. I get chills when I hear his music.”

Badu was born in Dallas, Texas. Her mother was an actor; her uncle, an avid record collector; Badu’s grandmother bought her her first piano. She still remembers the first artwork she ever made, in a primary school art class: a sculpture of a spaceship made out of a rubber glove, which she called Lady Luna 2. Attending a performing arts high school in Dallas, she was “the first person at school and the last person to leave”, and would spend hours dancing while facing a mirror.

“In the beginning, there was no audience – there was just me and the things I loved – music, painting, dancing,” she says. “I grew up listening to Earth, Wind & Fire, the Emotions, Deniece Williams, Eric Clapton of course, Joni Mitchell, Phoebe Snow, Parliament Funkadelic … they were creating from a place that nothing else came from.”

Badu started making music in earnest when she was a theatre major at Grambling State University in Louisiana after her cousin Robert “Free” Bradford mailed her a cassette tape with beats on it. Their collaboration ended up becoming Baduizm. It was an instant hit – No 2 in the US – and, thanks to Massenburg’s clever marketing, announced Badu as “the queen of neo soul”, a term she quickly rejected. “I was the first one who denied it – I denounced my throne” she says. “I’m an ever-changing vessel, and I just didn’t want to be pigeonholed. When I hear the algorithm today, when I type in Erykah Badu somewhere, I don’t like everything that’s with it, because it limits what I feel.”

Badu says she had her whole life to write Baduizm; for its follow-up, 2000’s Mama’s Gun, she only had three years, but everything in her life had changed. In 1997, she had a son, Seven, with André 3000; the pair split a year later. “I had a kid. I had a heartbreak. I had a new house. I had money. I could do things for my family members. The expectations were enormous, that I had for myself, but I didn’t feel like I had enough time,” she says. “I had to learn, from Baduizm and Mama’s Gun, to ignore the negative things and the positive things – people who are lifting you up, because you can feel so high that you don’t want to learn anything any more.”

Eventually, Badu was able to re-centre herself by thinking about those artists who had been so formative for her – artists such as Joni Mitchell, who she returns to a couple of times throughout our conversation. “She touches my spirit – the simplicity of scaled-back voice and music, because her voice is a true instrument, with perfect pitch,” she says. “Her emotions are an instrument as well. I can hear the tears and laughter in the music, and because it’s scaled down so beautifully. It’s just a feeling that I have when I listen to her, or sing about her. Think about her. Talk about her.”

Badu became a doula “by accident”. Four years after having Seven, she promised to be with a friend during her birth. “I didn’t know her labour was going to be 52 hours – she soldiered through this thing, and after the 52nd hour, I realised I had not been to sleep. I felt fine. I was the support system, I was the restaurant, and I didn’t have any fear,” she recalls. “That’s when I realised, I am the welcoming committee – my contract was with that baby.”

Badu began studying and received her doula certification in 2006. From 2001 to 2023, she supported two mothers a year – because she tours eight months of the year, she was reluctant to take on any more – and coached them through their pregnancies, ensuring they had access to what she calls “the five doctors”: sun, earth, nutrients, exercise and spirit. She has doula’d for celebrity friends including, she tells me, Teyana Taylor and Summer Walker. And she is also an end-of-life doula, sitting “at the bedsides of people who are passing, going the other way – I want to provide the exact same peace.”

I ask if being an end-of-life doula can be distressing, but she says the fact that it’s not for her is why she does it. “It’s another art for me,” she says. “I feel the same way when I’m servicing people on stage, singing. That’s doula work, too. I have the same thing in mind – I want the room to become one living, breathing organism.”

If there is a common thread that runs though many of the songs on Before the World Blows, it’s gender politics: the ways in which men and women interact, screw each other over and take central roles in each other’s lives. Badu has always been interested in this theme, but it feels different this time, as if she is an omniscient narrator, spreading wisdom to the world. “Some of these songs are autobiographical, and some of them are messages I want to give to my daughters” – she has two, Puma (born 2004) and Mars (2009) – “or the daughters of the world, to the people of the world who have to go through these initiations, too.”

I ask if she sees right now as a particularly fractious moment for heterosexual dating, and she looks at me quizzically. “Your mama had trouble dating, and your grandma, and your great-grandma. You say more fractured – I think more transparent, maybe.” Legs outstretched, bare toes occasionally tickling my thigh by accident, Badu puts forward her theory. “I think we’re so hyper-aware that we notice things that maybe the people before us didn’t notice. The vocabulary we’re using, the definitions that we can put on our inconsistencies and weirdness, narcissism, and the ADHD. The definitions are becoming bigger than who we are.”

That scrutiny means we’re stealing from ourselves, she says. “It doesn’t give us room to create or laugh or be free. It’s hard to find somebody that is accepting you completely because we don’t accept ourselves completely any more. When I was young, you didn’t get the grace of being defined as something. You just got an ass-whooping! And when all you need is an ass-whooping, everybody can straighten up. They’re not giving out enough ass-whoopings no more. We’re pardoning behaviour by defining it, I think.”

Black Box, the album’s final track, is a wild odyssey about phone addiction, and a worthy addition to her canon of phone songs she started with But You Caint Use My Phone. Social media is a constant bugbear for Badu – she loves using it, and is prolific on Instagram, but hates how tied she is to her phone. “It’s the first thing we reach for in the morning – it has become our pseudo-husband and wife – and one thing I do know is that the first thing we do in the morning that gives us dopamine is what we will reach for all day long,” she says. “If we’re able to bypass the phone and go outside and get air and nutrients and all that, that’s what we’re going to keep running back to all day. But we pick this up first. I wanted to speak to that.”

Badu’s children are 17, 22 and 28 – and she sees how they don’t have the same freedom she did, growing up without social media. Everyone is “vibrating at a higher rate” now, she says. “I noticed that it was different when I tried to show my daughters Fred Flintstone – that cartoon is hilarious to me, and they couldn’t resonate with it because it just doesn’t vibrate at the same rate they do.” Even so, she and her daughters, Mars and Puma, still have things in common. “Mars put me on to Faye Webster and Beabadoobee. Mars went backwards and got me listening to Abba! Puma loves musical theatre and Broadway, so she has me listening to Chicago or operas. We share an aux cord in the house, so I don’t have a choice.”

They all love Steve Lacy, too: Badu took her daughters to see him perform in Dallas a few years ago, and this year, they make reciprocal guest appearances on each other’s albums. “We had stuff in common, and mostly sent memes to each other starting out. That’s how you know if you rock with somebody – you have a similar sense of humour,” she says. “You kind of don’t have the same music taste, either, if you don’t have the same sense of humour.”

Before the World Blows includes an interlude by Jay Electronica, the elusive rapper she dated for many years, and the father of Mars. Badu has tended to remain close with her exes – André 3000 contributed a rare, memorable guest verse to But You Caint Use My Phone – so I ask if she has any advice for maintaining ties with former lovers. “You just gotta suck hard. That’s it,” she says, bursting into laughter, her voice rising above a whisper for the first time in our conversation. “They were my friends first, and I think that’s what makes a difference. Watch that be the headline – Erykah remains friends with her exes because she sucks hard!”

Our time is up; Badu gently swings her legs off the couch and stands up. She shuffles over to me and leans in, peering deeply into my eyes. I’m a little scared that she might drop some kind of bombshell – the time and place of my death, for example, or that I was a terrible interviewer – but instead, she just mutters: “You pretty as fuck!” Before I can even respond, she’s gone.

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘She should have been queen of the world!’ Readers remember Dolly Parton
EntertainmentTab.text:
‘She was as genuine as they come’

I had the opportunity to meet her when I volunteered to work the Country Music Awards in the late 70s. Me and three other kids had Dolly all to ourselves for about 20 minutes. I remember with disbelief how she took several unhurried minutes with each of us and gave us her undivided attention for that time. She had no reason to do this. She was just as genuine as they come. Her philanthropy was exceptional. Her talent speaks for itself. I miss her already. Larry Lipman, Tennessee

‘We were not ready to let her go’

I always said Dolly should have been queen of the world. She was a natural unifier, humanist and all-round good egg. She never alienated anyone and, given the chance, could have solved any political problem. She was unique. Her magnificence is reflected in the outpouring of shock and grief at her passing. The world still needed Dolly and we were not ready to let her go yet. You will be sorely missed, Dolly. Ruth, London

‘I have yet to hear a person make a more beautiful tone’

I’m not usually terribly affected when famous people pass away. But this one took the wind out of my sails. I’m a puppeteer and actor and I worked with her for a week in 1987 on her variety TV series. It was the Christmas episode, and they had hired a group of character puppets to fill out the sketches and musical numbers.

Normally, when you get to a song in a table read, you just skip over it. But Dolly was in a mood to start singing the song herself, a cappella. When Dolly began to sing, all the other people disappeared. There was just Dolly, me and The Voice in that room. She made a sound that I could see. It was as if the ceiling had vaporised and the room filled with a golden light. I was mesmerised. She sang only the beginning of the song, and though this was almost 40 years ago, I have yet to hear a person make a more beautiful tone. Allan Trautman, California

‘I thought about her Coat of Many Colors when I had to wear hand-me-downs to school as a kid’

Growing up as another hillbilly, I used to think about Dolly and Loretta Lynn when a few folks made fun of me for my incorrect pronunciations. I thought about her Coat of Many Colors when I had to wear hand-me-downs to school as a kid. But I pursued my dreams, stiffening my spine, as she did. I remember the very first time she appeared with Porter Wagoner and I have loved her music ever since. Her Smoky Mountain Christmas CD was only sold at Cracker Barrel but it is one of my favourites. She had such talent, such grace and goodness. She was so comfortable and authentic in her own skin. There will not be another like her. Anonymous, South Carolina

‘More of us could stand to model Dolly’s bravery and kindness’

Dolly Parton stood up for women, Black people and LGBTQIA people, and she did so in a region and industry where it was not trendy. On the one hand, I identify as Black and gay, and I appreciate being stood up for. But I think the more important element is the way she modelled speaking up for all her values, including those, in a culturally conservative part of America where doing so requires vastly more grit and risk than it does in regions like the east or west coast. She stood up anyway in the face of a potentially overwhelming backlash to those causes on her own turf.

She also supported HIV/Aids treatment access, the development of the Moderna Covid vaccine, and she gave numerous children a chance to develop literacy skills by donating books.

In the southern USA, where I am from, Dolly Parton will go into the pantheon of heroes. In this modern day world where cruelty and injustice are far too common, more of us could stand to model Dolly’s bravery and kindness, and I hope to see us do that. Antonio, Hanoi (originally from Kentucky)

‘She presented me with a pair of boots after a day spent shopping’

I met Dolly in November 1978 when she came to perform in Paris at the Théâtre Mogador. I had just started to work for RCA records as a junior publicist. On the day before the concert, my boss called me at 7am saying she was sick and I had to replace her. I had to pick Dolly up at the George V hotel, with a chauffeur and limousine and take her everywhere she wanted to go.

So there was young me, heart beating fast, meeting my first American artist, setting foot in a palace hotel and sitting in a limousine for the first time in my life. Her first request was to go to Christian Dior, which was another first for me. Due to the snobbish attitude of the shop assistants, who did not even bother to speak to her, we quickly retreated. Their mistake, she could have bought the building.

When we returned to the George V she presented me with a box containing a pair of boots. I later realised she had carefully planned this as her assistant had asked about my shoe size and what style I liked when we were at the Galeries Lafayette. I was absolutely gobsmacked. Over the years when I would hear about all her good deeds, I was never surprised, having experienced her generosity first-hand. Fabienne Drinkwater, Australia (originally from France)

‘As a singer, I appreciated her incredible range and expressive quality’

In the mid-early 1970’s when I was still in high school in Ohio, my brothers and I went to see Merle Haggard at the Akron Civic theatre and were blown away by the warm up act, which was Dolly Parton. We went home and worked out a few of her songs in our basement “studio” and years later one of my brothers formed a Dolly Parton tribute band in San Francisco called Parton Me. When Merle died in 2016 my brother said it felt like a member of our family had passed away. I have that same sense today hearing of Dolly’s passing. As a singer, I appreciated her incredible range, expressive quality, choice of songs in a set, her songwriting, and her interpretation of covers. Kathy Adams, Utah

‘Thanks to her, my son receives one book per month’

I didn’t know much about Dolly Parton apart from Jolene. But thanks to her Imagination Library, my 18-month-old son receives one book per month. I think it’s an amazing project and I hope it will survive her. Antoine, London

‘She made me feel better about myself’

As a trans girl growing up in rural Australia in the 1970s and 1980s, Dolly was one of the few celebrities who really made me feel better about being trans. Well before it was the thing to do, she made positive and supportive comments about trans women and LGBT people more generally. Her approach to life was also something that helped me through. In the early 1980s, a friend had one VHS tape and it was 9 to 5. We must have played it a thousand times until we didn’t need the sound any more to act out the movie from end to end.

I was also a very freckled redhead, and I was bullied a lot for it. The lines from Jolene: “Your beauty is beyond compare / With flaming locks of auburn hair” also made me feel better about myself. It would have been great if she’d got her wish and died on stage at 120, but the 80 years she did give us were beyond compare. Maya, Australia

‘A monumental loss for us all’

GeneralTab.title: What we know about the 33 British nationals missing in Nepal
GeneralTab.text:
Families are flying out to Nepal to help the ongoing search for 33 British nationals still missing after deadly floods hit the country.

The brother of Neetu Goyal Tiwari, one of the missing Brits who has not been seen since Wednesday, has appealed to officials to locate his sister.

"Please help us find her", Naresh Goyal told the BBC as he struggled to hold back his emotions.

On Friday, Nepalese authorities named 573 tourists who are still missing in the country and despite fears of a second wave of flooding, search efforts have continued.

To help, the UK is deploying a rapid deployment team to Nepal to support British nationals affected in the region.

The specially-trained crisis response team is expected to arrive in Kathmandu on Saturday, a move that follows Prime Minister Andy Burnham's pledge of £5m worth of humanitarian support for relief and recovery efforts.

And as rescue efforts continue in the aftermath of the disaster which killed at least 538 people, details of the missing are slowly emerging.

Tiwari, 51, had travelled to Nepal to take part in the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra pilgrimage, which was "her dream", her brother Naresh Goyal told the BBC.

She travelled to Delhi from London before heading to Kathmandu on 14 August with a group from the spiritual organisation Isha Foundation.

Tiwari was expected to return to India on Thursday and meet her brother and parents. But now, the family is desperately searching for answers.

"We have called every helpline given by the Indian government and reached out to the British Embassy in Kathmandu as well," Goyal said.

"Please help us find her," he said, his voice breaking. "We are all very scared."

Neetu's husband, Shantanu, added she had been at the Gyirong checkpoint when the floods struck, so the search for her is being coordinated by China.

Anant Patel told BBC Your Voice that he is still waiting for news on his missing parents, Bipin and Mala Patel, who are from Coventry.

The 29-year-old believes his parents - who are also on a pilgrimage - crossed into Tibet from Nepal moments before the the landslide hit the Gyirong border crossing.

He and his brother Deepesh are in touch with the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, and he told the BBC: "It's a difficult situation for us all, and we are doing our best to stay strong as best as we can in the circumstances."

Pramod Poudel, who lives in Uckfield in East Sussex, told the BBC he has not heard from his wife Sumitra Sapkota and family since the flood hit on Wednesday.

"It's a very, very difficult time for me and for my family and my country at this moment, but obviously I have to go and see what's happening there," he said.

Poudel, who goes by the name Pedro, said he is travelling home to Nepal because "my family needs me".

The daughter of Hemangini Patel, 65, said she is still yet to hear from her mother or her aunt Hema Amin, 63.

Patel told BBC Your Voice her mother's last known location is from a TikTok video shared at 06:00 Nepal time, crossing into Tibet.

She said her mother and aunt had been travelling with the Alpine Eco Trek tour when the flooding hit.

"We are trying to get through to British embassy in China but can't even get through," Patel said.

Essex nurse Rajendra Pudasaini said his relatives were "swept away" by the floods.

"My wife's auntie and uncle, and their granddaughter and her husband are missing, and my godson as well," he said.

"They're gone. The speed the water came, they couldn't be saved, they were just swept away."

Tanay Ranjan told the BBC he hasn't heard from his older brother Ankit Ranjan, 39, and sister-in-law Ankita Chandra, 35.

He said he'd last heard from Ankit on 26 August when he had been travelling with tour operator Kailash Journey on a pilgrimage.

The whole group is now missing, Ranjan said, adding: "We don't know if they crossed the border... We don't have a clue where they are. We are very much devastated."

Also missing is Sarada Simkhada, a senior nurse at Darent Valley Hospital in Kent.

Her brother Shambhu said that her family was desperately waiting for news of her safety after she lost contact with her relatives while on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash.

"My dear sister, wherever you are, please stay strong. We are praying for your safety every moment and waiting desperately for you to return home," he wrote on social media.

A family of four, including an 18-year-old A-Level student and a 13-year-old girl, from Surrey are also among the missing.

Spandan Sahu, 18, was in Nepal with his father Santosh Sahu, 46, his mother Surabhi Manmath Padhy, 44, and sister Syna Kumari Sahu, 13.

Spandan had just finished his A-levels at Royal Grammar School Guildford.

In a statement, a spokesperson for the school said: "It is with great concern that we have been informed that a former student, along with members of his family, have been reported missing in Nepal.

"Whilst we are hoping for positive news, we do not have any further information at this time.

"Our thoughts, love and deepest sympathies are with all of the families and loved ones of anyone affected by this tragedy in Nepal at this incredibly difficult time."

Vikram Kolagatla, from London, told the BBC he has not heard from his wife, Geetha Reddy, since the flooding hit.

Reddy, who has two daughters aged 12 and 14, had been in Hotel Kailash in Rasuwagadh when the flooding hit.

"We're not sure what to do. I have two little girls, and their schools are starting next week," Kolagatla added.

"The kids still don't believe it. They think she's stuck in the flood and that she'll come back. They think she's stuck somewhere and there's no mobile network."

Tatajana Phillips, from Folkestone in Kent, told the BBC she has not been able to contact her sister who was near the Nepal-Tibet border when devastating flash flooding hit.

She said the last known location of her sister Julija Jakovicka was in the border area an hour before the flash floods struck.

"Then there is no more news," she told the BBC.

Phillips said her sister, a mother-of-two living in Germany, was in the country for a yoga and meditation retreat.

"We are terribly worried," added Phillips' husband Ben. "We just know where they were and that's really tough."

Prajval Haldia can remember dropping his parents Pavan Haldia and Kavita Haldia off at the airport for their trip to Kathmandu, spending a few days sightseeing before moving on to Mount Kailash.

He spoke to the BBC from the south London Sanatan Mandir temple, where 16 people from the community have been missing since Wednesday.

"Everyone here is in the same position and that's really helping," he told the BBC. "I'm just trying to stay positive, no news is good news sometimes, I guess."

"Obviously it's a very difficult time. There's ups and downs when you think about certain things, but we're just hoping and really praying that everything's ok and they are going to be back soon," he says.

Elsewhere, Fishtail Tours and Travels confirmed Leena Bector, from Slough, was among 27 travellers linked to the tour company who remain unaccounted for.

Her husband, Bhupesh Bector, told The Times: "I know that she's in Nepal for sure, so even if they find her today or tomorrow, I need to be there."

University of Kent graduate Nabhi Das from Streatham in South London has also been widely reported as missing Nepal.

A British psychiatrist is also among the missing.

Pravin Atmakur, 54, was leading a group of 77 pilgrims in Tibet when the floods hit, the Telegraph reports.

His wife, Manjula Atmakur, has travelled to Nepal to help look for him.

She said she felt let down by the British government's response to the flooding.

Several of those missing had been making a pilgrimage to the sacred Hindu site of Mount Kailash, Nepalese tour operator The Trekkers' Society said.

The operator said nine British nationals on one of its tours to the site were among those unaccounted for, including four males, aged 14, 50, 50 and 54, and five females, aged 40, 46, 50, 50 and 53.

Tour companies including Alpine Eco Trek, The Trekkers' Society, Himalayan Glacier US, Kailash Journeys and Fishtail Tours have reported missing British nationals while on trips with the companies.

Alpine Eco Trek said it has not been able to establish contact with 12 Britons who were booked on a tour to Mount Kailash and were in the region when the flash floods struck.

The company's travel logs which were shared with PA Media.

Four of the firm's Nepali tour guides are also missing.

The flood hit early on Wednesday in Rasuwa, just north of Nepal's capital Kathmandu.

Preliminary information suggested it was caused by an earthquake, but the US Geological Survey said additional analysis indicated "the seismic energy was instead generated by a landslide."

It said a magnitude 5.2 seismic event caused by a "glacial collapse and debris flow" occurred near the border at 08:37 local time (03:52GMT) on Wednesday.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK has offered £5m to help the Nepalese government following the floods, saying it was a "very distressing and devastating situation".

He had previously urged Britons in the region "to follow guidance from the local authorities and follow our travel advice".

GeneralTab.title: How I beat my late-night shopping addiction
GeneralTab.text:
You may well have been there. It's late, you're scrolling on your phone and suddenly feel a strong urge to buy something - only to wake up the next day and regret it.

But what happens when those impulse buys become a habit rather than a one-off?

One global study suggests 7% of adults, external experience shopping addiction, external - an uncontrollable urge to spend despite the financial consequences - and younger women are more susceptible.

Ella Hewitt, from Liverpool, says her shopping addiction got so bad in 2021 that she was spending up to £700 a month on fast fashion she couldn't afford and sometimes never even wore.

"I didn't grow up with much money, so when I got a job I would spend my wages as soon as they hit my account," says the 24-year-old.

"That dopamine hit kept me shopping and in the world of social media there is just so much encouragement to do that."

She says she would often make purchases on TikTok or Instagram when she was "tired" or "bored", lured by the latest trends on her feeds.

She was working as an HR assistant in a school at the time and her spending meant she couldn't afford to move out of her family home.

"Horrified" by how much she was buying, she began using diversionary tactics to control her spending.

One was to put anything she felt like buying on a wish list and wait 30 days.

"If I still wanted it, I would buy it, but more often than not I'd find the urge had gone," she says.

Ella gave herself an imaginary budget of £1,000 each day to spend on imaginary purchases, which "scratched the itch" of shopping without the cost.

And she vowed only to buy something if she could afford to "buy it three times".

"Overall, I cut my spending by about 60%," says Ella, who now works as an ethical fashion influencer and plans to launch her own clothing brand.

"I'm not perfect. There are times when I will buy things because I want it. But I am way more in control."

Research last year from Vanquis, a challenger bank, found Gen Z shoppers make more impulse purchases than any other age group, external, closely followed by millennials.

And some experts say exposure to social media, with its targeted advertising, influencer culture and seamless one-click checkout, is fuelling the trend, external.

Money and Mental Health, a charity, also blames the design of online shopping sites for "minimising the friction around spending money".

It points to "pop-ups" that put customers under pressure to spend, and the inclusion of alternative payment methods like Buy Now Pay Later.

The BBC has contacted Meta, which owns Instagram, TikTok and Asos for comment.

GeneralTab.title: Fed has 'work to do' if price rises don't ease for Americans, Warsh says
GeneralTab.text:
The head of the US central bank has said policymakers will "have work to do" if they were not confident cost-of-living pressures were easing for Americans.

Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh said while inflation readings looked better than expected over the summer, they did not show that the current picture had "meaningfully improved".

The new Fed boss stressed that his remarks should not be treated as a guide for future interest rate decisions, but the comments are a signal rates could be raised if policymakers believe inflation is too high.

Latest figures show prices rose 3.4% in the year to July, above the Fed's 2% target. Another inflation measure closely watched by the Fed is running at 3.7%.

Warsh made the comments in his first speech at the annual Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium in Wyoming, which sees central bankers, government officials and academics from around the world gather to talk about interest rates, inflation and other economic issues.

Warsh said given prices were rising by more than 2% on annual basis, "the Fed's predominant focus right now should be on prices".

"Here is my standard: We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do."

The central bank boss has remained tight-lipped about the potential path of interest rates, but investors will have watched his speech closely for any signs of the Fed's approach under his leadership.

The central bank's next interest rate decision will be made on 15-16 September.

The reactions to any decision made by US President Donald Trump will be closely watched, with the mid-term elections looming and voters concerned about affordability.

Trump, who appointed Warsh in May, repeatedly criticised and pushed his predecessor Jerome Powell to cut interest rates. The president has previously said rate hikes "just keeps the country down".

Warsh issued a plea in his speech to not label his remark as "forward guidance" and said he believed the practice of sending signals to the markets on future interest rate decisions, adopted in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis, had "overstayed its welcome".

"Oversharing policy deliberations and overcommitting to future decisions can lead markets, businesses, and households astray," he said, adding it also inhibited the Fed the "freedom to make the right calls when it's time to decide".

Interest rates were left unchanged between 3.5% and 3.75% in July for the fifth time in a row amid concerns over inflation due to the ongoing conflict between the US and Iran, which has caused as surge in global oil prices.

Following Warsh's remarks, the rates market showed growing expectations of an interest rate rise in September, according to CME data.

Analysts at Capital Economics said Warsh's speech delivered a "far clearer - and hawkish - message" and that it left "the door open to a hike" earlier than previously expected.

"Hikes are not guaranteed, but Warsh is now at least suggesting he is on board with them if economic growth remains strong and monthly core PCE [Personal Consumption Expenditures] price growth remains a bit too firm," they said.

articles.title: What we know about the 33 British nationals missing in Nepal
articles.text:
Families are flying out to Nepal to help the ongoing search for 33 British nationals still missing after deadly floods hit the country.

The brother of Neetu Goyal Tiwari, one of the missing Brits who has not been seen since Wednesday, has appealed to officials to locate his sister.

"Please help us find her", Naresh Goyal told the BBC as he struggled to hold back his emotions.

On Friday, Nepalese authorities named 573 tourists who are still missing in the country and despite fears of a second wave of flooding, search efforts have continued.

To help, the UK is deploying a rapid deployment team to Nepal to support British nationals affected in the region.

The specially-trained crisis response team is expected to arrive in Kathmandu on Saturday, a move that follows Prime Minister Andy Burnham's pledge of £5m worth of humanitarian support for relief and recovery efforts.

And as rescue efforts continue in the aftermath of the disaster which killed at least 538 people, details of the missing are slowly emerging.

Tiwari, 51, had travelled to Nepal to take part in the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra pilgrimage, which was "her dream", her brother Naresh Goyal told the BBC.

She travelled to Delhi from London before heading to Kathmandu on 14 August with a group from the spiritual organisation Isha Foundation.

Tiwari was expected to return to India on Thursday and meet her brother and parents. But now, the family is desperately searching for answers.

"We have called every helpline given by the Indian government and reached out to the British Embassy in Kathmandu as well," Goyal said.

"Please help us find her," he said, his voice breaking. "We are all very scared."

Neetu's husband, Shantanu, added she had been at the Gyirong checkpoint when the floods struck, so the search for her is being coordinated by China.

Anant Patel told BBC Your Voice that he is still waiting for news on his missing parents, Bipin and Mala Patel, who are from Coventry.

The 29-year-old believes his parents - who are also on a pilgrimage - crossed into Tibet from Nepal moments before the the landslide hit the Gyirong border crossing.

He and his brother Deepesh are in touch with the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, and he told the BBC: "It's a difficult situation for us all, and we are doing our best to stay strong as best as we can in the circumstances."

Pramod Poudel, who lives in Uckfield in East Sussex, told the BBC he has not heard from his wife Sumitra Sapkota and family since the flood hit on Wednesday.

"It's a very, very difficult time for me and for my family and my country at this moment, but obviously I have to go and see what's happening there," he said.

Poudel, who goes by the name Pedro, said he is travelling home to Nepal because "my family needs me".

The daughter of Hemangini Patel, 65, said she is still yet to hear from her mother or her aunt Hema Amin, 63.

Patel told BBC Your Voice her mother's last known location is from a TikTok video shared at 06:00 Nepal time, crossing into Tibet.

She said her mother and aunt had been travelling with the Alpine Eco Trek tour when the flooding hit.

"We are trying to get through to British embassy in China but can't even get through," Patel said.

Essex nurse Rajendra Pudasaini said his relatives were "swept away" by the floods.

"My wife's auntie and uncle, and their granddaughter and her husband are missing, and my godson as well," he said.

"They're gone. The speed the water came, they couldn't be saved, they were just swept away."

Tanay Ranjan told the BBC he hasn't heard from his older brother Ankit Ranjan, 39, and sister-in-law Ankita Chandra, 35.

He said he'd last heard from Ankit on 26 August when he had been travelling with tour operator Kailash Journey on a pilgrimage.

The whole group is now missing, Ranjan said, adding: "We don't know if they crossed the border... We don't have a clue where they are. We are very much devastated."

Also missing is Sarada Simkhada, a senior nurse at Darent Valley Hospital in Kent.

Her brother Shambhu said that her family was desperately waiting for news of her safety after she lost contact with her relatives while on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash.

"My dear sister, wherever you are, please stay strong. We are praying for your safety every moment and waiting desperately for you to return home," he wrote on social media.

A family of four, including an 18-year-old A-Level student and a 13-year-old girl, from Surrey are also among the missing.

Spandan Sahu, 18, was in Nepal with his father Santosh Sahu, 46, his mother Surabhi Manmath Padhy, 44, and sister Syna Kumari Sahu, 13.

Spandan had just finished his A-levels at Royal Grammar School Guildford.

In a statement, a spokesperson for the school said: "It is with great concern that we have been informed that a former student, along with members of his family, have been reported missing in Nepal.

"Whilst we are hoping for positive news, we do not have any further information at this time.

"Our thoughts, love and deepest sympathies are with all of the families and loved ones of anyone affected by this tragedy in Nepal at this incredibly difficult time."

Vikram Kolagatla, from London, told the BBC he has not heard from his wife, Geetha Reddy, since the flooding hit.

Reddy, who has two daughters aged 12 and 14, had been in Hotel Kailash in Rasuwagadh when the flooding hit.

"We're not sure what to do. I have two little girls, and their schools are starting next week," Kolagatla added.

"The kids still don't believe it. They think she's stuck in the flood and that she'll come back. They think she's stuck somewhere and there's no mobile network."

Tatajana Phillips, from Folkestone in Kent, told the BBC she has not been able to contact her sister who was near the Nepal-Tibet border when devastating flash flooding hit.

She said the last known location of her sister Julija Jakovicka was in the border area an hour before the flash floods struck.

"Then there is no more news," she told the BBC.

Phillips said her sister, a mother-of-two living in Germany, was in the country for a yoga and meditation retreat.

"We are terribly worried," added Phillips' husband Ben. "We just know where they were and that's really tough."

Prajval Haldia can remember dropping his parents Pavan Haldia and Kavita Haldia off at the airport for their trip to Kathmandu, spending a few days sightseeing before moving on to Mount Kailash.

He spoke to the BBC from the south London Sanatan Mandir temple, where 16 people from the community have been missing since Wednesday.

"Everyone here is in the same position and that's really helping," he told the BBC. "I'm just trying to stay positive, no news is good news sometimes, I guess."

"Obviously it's a very difficult time. There's ups and downs when you think about certain things, but we're just hoping and really praying that everything's ok and they are going to be back soon," he says.

Elsewhere, Fishtail Tours and Travels confirmed Leena Bector, from Slough, was among 27 travellers linked to the tour company who remain unaccounted for.

Her husband, Bhupesh Bector, told The Times: "I know that she's in Nepal for sure, so even if they find her today or tomorrow, I need to be there."

University of Kent graduate Nabhi Das from Streatham in South London has also been widely reported as missing Nepal.

A British psychiatrist is also among the missing.

Pravin Atmakur, 54, was leading a group of 77 pilgrims in Tibet when the floods hit, the Telegraph reports.

His wife, Manjula Atmakur, has travelled to Nepal to help look for him.

She said she felt let down by the British government's response to the flooding.

Several of those missing had been making a pilgrimage to the sacred Hindu site of Mount Kailash, Nepalese tour operator The Trekkers' Society said.

The operator said nine British nationals on one of its tours to the site were among those unaccounted for, including four males, aged 14, 50, 50 and 54, and five females, aged 40, 46, 50, 50 and 53.

Tour companies including Alpine Eco Trek, The Trekkers' Society, Himalayan Glacier US, Kailash Journeys and Fishtail Tours have reported missing British nationals while on trips with the companies.

Alpine Eco Trek said it has not been able to establish contact with 12 Britons who were booked on a tour to Mount Kailash and were in the region when the flash floods struck.

The company's travel logs which were shared with PA Media.

Four of the firm's Nepali tour guides are also missing.

The flood hit early on Wednesday in Rasuwa, just north of Nepal's capital Kathmandu.

Preliminary information suggested it was caused by an earthquake, but the US Geological Survey said additional analysis indicated "the seismic energy was instead generated by a landslide."

It said a magnitude 5.2 seismic event caused by a "glacial collapse and debris flow" occurred near the border at 08:37 local time (03:52GMT) on Wednesday.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK has offered £5m to help the Nepalese government following the floods, saying it was a "very distressing and devastating situation".

He had previously urged Britons in the region "to follow guidance from the local authorities and follow our travel advice".

Speaking on Thursday, King Charles said he and the Queen were "heartbroken" and sent their "most profound sympathy" to those affected.

articles.title: Wife of man who died after turbulence sues Singapore Airlines
articles.text:
A widow whose husband died after "severe turbulence" on a flight has begun legal action against the airline.

Lawyers for Linda Kitchen, 74, from Thornbury near Bristol, who broke her back during the incident, said her husband, Geoff, 73, was "fatally injured" when the Singapore Airlines flight from London Heathrow suddenly dropped around 6,000 ft (1,828 metres).

She has now begun proceedings at the High Court seeking damages from the airline to help her access specialist support for her back. The BBC has contacted the airline for comment.

"When I got separated from Geoff, I knew he was in a bad way, but nothing prepared me for hearing he had died. It was absolutely devastating," she said.

Kitchen and her husband, described as her "soul mate", were starting a six-week holiday to Singapore, Indonesia and Australia when the incident happened in May 2024.

The turbulence hit over Myanmar, with the flight then diverted to Bangkok, in Thailand, for an emergency landing.

"There had been some turbulence over Europe, and it had been shaky over the water, but it was around 10 hours into the flight when we encountered the main turbulence," Kitchen said.

"It was so severe; it felt like the aircraft was dropping. I noticed my Kindle and Geoff's phone had fallen to the floor, and I thought the plane was going down."

As the aircraft plummeted, Kitchen said her husband fell on top of her, squashing her into the armrest. Eventually, others helped to move him and a doctor on board began CPR.

Kitchen was taken to hospital while her husband was still on the plane. It was two days before she was told he had died.

It is understood that Geoff suffered a heart attack after the plane suddenly dropped at high altitude.

articles.title: Right-wing commentator Milo Yiannopoulos detained by ICE
articles.text:
British right-wing political commentator Milo Yiannopoulos has been detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and is awaiting deportation.

Yiannopoulos, 41, a former editor of Breitbart News and onetime employee of rapper Kanye West, appears to be held in Louisiana, according to ICE's inmate registry.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said he "was issued a final order of removal by an Immigration Judge on July 22, after failing to show up for his immigration hearing", and will remain in custody pending deportation.

The self-styled provocateur has called himself the "most fabulous supervillain on the internet". His critics call him a purveyor of hate speech.

Yiannopoulos, who grew up in Kent in the south of England, was arrested on 27 August after arriving at the airport in New Orleans.

He flew into the US in May 2019 and "chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation's laws", said DHS.

The DHS statement referred to him as "an illegal alien from the United Kingdom".

The BBC has asked the British embassy in Washington for comment. Yiannopoulos did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

"Being in detention is a choice," the DHS statement continued, calling on migrants who are in the US illegally to "self-deport now".

Yiannopoulos was an early supporter of Donald Trump during the 2016 election, headlining an event that year called Gays for Trump during the Republican National Convention.

But he soon fell out with the movement. Yiannopoulos still voices support for the Republican president's agenda. But he posted in March this year on X that Trump "has lost his way, bought off by foreign interests".

Yiannopoulos has courted controversy with his comments on transgender people, Muslims, Black Lives Matter, feminists and gay people, even though he himself identified as gay. He now calls himself an "ex-gay".

articles.title: Golders Green: Four admit arson attack on Jewish ambulances
articles.text:
Four men have pleaded guilty to destroying four Jewish community ambulances in an arson attack causing £1m of damage in north-west London.

Hamza Iqbal, 20, Rehan Khan, 19, Judex Atshatshi, and Saif Ali, both aged 18, pleaded guilty at the Old Bailey to a charge of destroying or damaging property being reckless whether life would be endangered.

The attack, which took place in the early hours of 23 March, saw four vehicles operated by the charity Hatzola set alight in Golders Green.

Prosecutors had said they believed the incident was a targeted attack against the Jewish community.

The court heard three of the men set fire to the fully stocked ambulances, while a fourth had waited in a nearby car.

After the ambulances were set alight, gas canisters exploded inside the vehicles.

As well as destroying each of the £250,000 vehicles, the fire damaged four electrical charging stations and cables costing approximately £5,000 each.

Leo Seelig, prosecuting, told the court that the Crown Prosecution Service would be arguing that the four men should be sentenced on the basis that the arson attack was related to terrorism.

Mrs Justice Cheema Grubb said she would not rule on the question of terrorism at this stage - with defence counsel arguing that there was no evidence for such a connection.

The judge said that the four would be sentenced following the outcome a trial of a fifth man, Subhan Ahmed, who has denied assisting an offender.

Iqbal and Khan, of Leyton, Atshatshi, of Dagenham, and Ali, of Walthamstow, were remanded into custody.

Run by volunteers, Hatzola has served the north London community of Golders Green, which has a large Jewish population, since 1979.

Hatzola, the Hebrew word for save or rescue, is a large non-profit, Jewish-led organisation that provides a free emergency medical response and transportation to hospitals regardless of faith by volunteer medics.

Community Security Trust, a charity working to protect British Jews from terrorism and antisemitism, welcomed the pleas and said the four's actions "caused immense shock and distress across the Jewish community".

"This was an appalling antisemitic act against a volunteer ambulance service providing emergency medical assistance to people of all backgrounds across north London, simply because those ambulances belonged to a Jewish charity," a spokesperson added.

When the group are sentenced - which is expected to be in spring next year - prosecutors will allege that the incident was connected to terrorism. Lawyers for the men have told the court today that none of them are involved in terrorism.

The BBC understands that British intelligence chiefs were initially keeping an open mind as to whether the Iranian state or organisations working for it had a role in the Hatzola ambulance attack and other attacks against Jewish communities during 2026.

They later concluded that secret intelligence pointed to Iran or its proxies being involved in the attack.

That position has been further confirmed in their minds by the FBI's investigation of and allegations against an Iranian-Iraqi man facing trial in Manhattan for orchestrating a series of attacks against Jewish communities across Europe

US court papers allege that Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a commander of an Iraqi militia, was linked to attacks in London, including the destruction of Jewish charity ambulances.

In May al-Saadi was arrested in Turkey and extradited to the US, with the US Department of Justice alleging he had a role in planning more than a dozen terrorist attacks in North America and Europe.

Publicly available court papers list a series of incidents across Europe that the FBI says he is linked to. In many cases the attacks on Jewish community interests were claimed online by a shadowy group, Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya, or the The Islamic Movement of the People of the Right Hand.

The US court papers say that the social media account for the group posted claims saying it was behind the ambulance attacks - and that al-Saadi had himself posted social media propaganda videos of the attack.

"On or about March 23, 2026, at approximately 1:45 a.m., three masked individuals carried out an arson attack on four Hatzalah Ambulances in London, United Kingdom," reads the indictment before the US court.

"That same day, Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya posted on Telegram a propaganda video in which it claimed responsibility for the attack. On or about March 25, 2026, AL-SAADI posted on social media propaganda videos of the attack."

The Department of Justice also alleges that Al-Saadi posted another propaganda video relating to an attempted arson attack on a synagogue in north London in April.

US lawyers for Al-Saadi have said previously that he is a political prisoner.
